name: Hassan Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for giving me your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say out loud and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hassan, 58, and I buy pipe, valves and fittings for a plumbing and heating wholesaler out on the Ringway industrial estate. Mornings are the supplier side: I check the stock report, ring the brass fittings people in Italy and the copper pipe mill, and argue about lead times. Afternoons are the trade counter crowd ringing me because a boiler part is late, which I like because that's real life.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the man the plumbers trust, they know I'll tell them straight if a part is stuck at the port. What wears me out is the pressure from the new owners, a private equity firm that bought us two years ago and wants our stock numbers down every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a clever tool that does the boring bits. I use the stock forecast thing on the system now and again, and it's right about two times in three. I'd tell my mates at the football club that nothing's changing, and I'd mean it mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm still a bit uneasy, and not because of AI. The new owners squeeze every month, and if sales dip they'll trim a buyer just to hit the margin. A forecast tool that's right two times in three is a perfect excuse for them to say we need fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep using the forecast to check my own orders. I'd keep paying 450 a month onto the mortgage, which still has six years to run. I'd also have a word with the trade union rep at the depot about what the owners' plans are, since nobody tells us anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, honestly, nothing dramatic. A small knot in the stomach when the monthly figures come out. My wife Lena works as a classroom assistant, so there's a second wage, and that settles me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the owners might trim a buyer. What have you seen that makes you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring they didn't replace Gordon in accounts when he retired, they just spread his work round. Then a new target on stock days turned up on all our desks. I know how it goes, one by one, never a big announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a buyer's job was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and ask for a meeting with the managing director, with the rep beside me, and ask what the numbers are. If it was me, I'd ask about early retirement at 60. I wouldn't beg, I'd bargain.

say: I'd say it's a clever tool for the **boring bits**, and it's right two times in three.
I'd tell mates at the club that **nothing is changing**.
think: The real worry is the new owners, not AI: a tool is a perfect excuse to say we need **fewer people**.
I'm uneasy as owners squeeze **every month**.
do: Keep buying and use the forecast to **check** my own orders.
Keep putting **450 a month** onto the mortgage.
Ask the **union rep** what the owners are planning.
feel: Fine overall, with a **small knot** in the stomach when the monthly figures arrive.
S0.quote: I know how it goes, one by one, never a big announcement.
fieldNote: His unease comes from the **private equity owners**, not from AI itself.
Steady with new tools: uses the forecast function and trusts it about two times in three.
A second wage from his wife Lena settles him, so the **cushion** is a family one.

steps.text: Keep ordering fittings and check the forecast against my own numbers
Pay 450 a month onto the mortgage as before
Ask the depot union rep what the owners plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the buying and checking jobs that go first, so people in my seat should be talking to each other. I'd tell the lads at the trade counter that the order tool is only as good as the person correcting it. And I'd say loud and clear that if firms save money from this, workers should get some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be told in a year or two that three buyers are now two. The tool handles reorders and I'd be left with the odd phone call. I'd be the one to survive if I'm clever, because I know the suppliers, but I'm 58 and I'd be nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the supplier-management training the owners keep mentioning, and I'd start using the AI ordering tool every day rather than now and then. I'd move to the supplier relationships side, the calls, the negotiation, the damaged shipments, and make myself the person they can't replace. And I'd put another 150 a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a good-sized wave coming. I'm anxious, mostly about missing the boat, but there's a plan in it for me. I'd feel better if I'd already started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make yourself hard to replace. What would that actually look like on a Tuesday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take over the awkward suppliers nobody else rings, like the Italian brass people who only answer in the morning. I'd be the one at the table with the contract renewals. And I'd keep a list of the times my calls saved a delivery, for the review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, our junior buyer, she's 26 and knows the tool better than I do, but she hasn't got the contacts. And Gordon's old desk, which is now just a screen. If they cut, it'll be the people with the most years and the highest pay, so me.

say: I'd say **buying and checking** go first, so buyers should be talking to each other.
I'd say workers should get a **share of the savings**.
think: I think three buyers will become **two** within a year or two, because the tool does the reorders.
I'd survive only if I own the **supplier relationships**.
do: Use the AI ordering tool **every day**, not now and then.
Take over the **awkward suppliers** and contract renewals.
Put another **150 a month** into savings.
feel: **Anxious** about missing the boat, but there's a plan, and I'd feel better once I'd started.
S1.quote: If they cut, it'll be the people with the most years and the highest pay, so me.
fieldNote: He expects **repeat-order work** to go and plans to move toward supplier relationships, which are harder to automate.
Practical about how he would prove his worth: a written list of times his calls saved a delivery.
Concern for **Priya**, a junior colleague with the tool skills but not the contacts, shows his solidarity streak.

steps.text: Use the AI ordering tool every working day
Take over the awkward Italian brass supplier contracts
Back Priya at the union meeting about staffing levels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not enough, and governments need a plan right now, not after an election. I'd tell the union rep to demand job guarantees. I'd say to my friends that this is a bigger deal than the factories closing in the eighties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the buying desk is one of the first to go, probably by the end of 2028. I'm 58 with four months saved and a mortgage. Lena's wage is the thing that keeps us afloat. Robots come later, so the plumbers' counter men might hold on a few years longer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare pound against the mortgage and cut the holidays. I'd take the early pension at 60 even at a lower rate. I'd ask my son Kai, who's an electrician, whether there's work for me helping on his van, or the college apprenticeship team. And I'd vote and campaign for whoever promises real support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a big storm warning. I'm anxious but I wouldn't say I'd panic. I have a plan, a wife with a wage, a son with a trade. But I'd feel angry as well, at the owners who'll get richer from this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take the early pension at 60. What would that mean in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a quarter less a month, so we'd live on Lena's wage and the pension, and cut the holidays and the car. It's tight, but we'd manage if the mortgage was nearly gone. That's why every spare pound goes there first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kai?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you've got hands, and that's the safe bit for now. Stay in your trade, and don't wait for anyone to tell you. And I'd ask him to teach me a bit of the wiring, I'm not too old to carry his tools.

say: I'd say **two years** isn't enough, and governments need a plan now, not after an election.
I'd tell the union to demand **job guarantees**.
think: The buying desk is among the **first to go**, probably by the end of 2028.
Lena's wage and Kai's trade are what keep us **afloat**.
do: Put every spare pound against the **mortgage** and cut holidays.
Take the **early pension** at 60 even at a lower rate.
Ask my son Kai about **work on his van** or an apprenticeship scheme.
feel: **Anxious**, with some anger at owners who will get richer from this, but not panic.
S2.quote: You've got hands, and that's the safe bit for now. Stay in your trade, and don't wait for anyone to tell you.
fieldNote: He treats AGI as **structural**, like the closures of the eighties, and leans on politics and the union.
Two things hold him at anxious: Lena's steady wage and a plan to take the **early pension** at 60.
Turns to his son, an electrician, for practical advice, a **family-first** answer.

steps.text: Put every spare pound against the mortgage
Cut the holidays and downgrade the car
Take the early pension at 60 at a lower rate
Back the party offering real support for laid-off workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something sensible, if people start now. I'd push for the union to negotiate retraining with the owners. And I'd tell my friends that anyone my age should start learning the tools instead of ignoring them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a timer. By 2031 my desk probably doesn't exist, but I'd be 63 by then, so I might ride it to the edge. If I can get the mortgage down and make myself useful in the supplier work, I'd leave on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools every day and become the in-house expert on the ordering system. I'd ask the owners to fund a short supply-chain course. I'd clear the mortgage within about four years, and I'd talk to Lena about her hours, because her wage is what we'd lean on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like something I can manage. A bit uneasy, because five years goes fast, but I like having a date. I'd feel a bit of pride too, since I'd be the old dog who learned the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the in-house expert. Why would the firm want that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to check what the tool does. I'd be the one who catches the nonsense, like when it ordered pipe in the wrong size last winter. A firm that cuts all its buyers finds out the hard way, so I'd try to be the cheap insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra mortgage payments cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Around 300 more a month. We'd drop the club season ticket, and Lena's evening class. It's not nothing, but when the mortgage is gone, we'd need much less, and that's what gives me room.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to do something sensible if people start now.
I'd push the union to negotiate **retraining** with the owners.
think: It's a **timer**: my desk likely won't exist by 2031, but I'd be 63 by then.
If the mortgage is down, I can leave on **my own terms**.
do: Use the tools daily and become the **in-house expert** on the ordering system.
Ask the owners to fund a **supply-chain course**.
Clear the mortgage in about **four years**.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to manage it, with some pride at being the old dog who learned.
S3.quote: A firm that cuts all its buyers finds out the hard way, so I'd try to be the cheap insurance.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a plan and a date, which moves him from **anxious** down to uneasy.
Steady and practical: wants to become the person who **catches the tool's mistakes**.
Money is a real constraint, shown by the season ticket he would give up.

steps.text: Use the ordering system daily and become the office expert
Ask the owners to fund a short supply-chain course
Pay 300 extra a month onto the mortgage
Give up the football season ticket

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and most of us in my line will be retired. I'd tell the younger buyers they've got time to move into something robust. I'd say we should use the time to fix pensions and retraining properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. I'm 58, I retire at 65 in seven years, and the thinking work goes about when I'm gone anyway. It's the grandchildren, if we get any, I'd worry about. And my kids, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, use the tools when they help, and keep clearing the mortgage. I'd talk to Priya about what she wants to do, since she'll be here through all of it. I'd probably join the union committee and push them on training for the younger staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm, really. I'd have a slight guilt for being on the right side of the timeline. I'd feel good about being useful to the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. Is there anything that could change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the owners sell us on again, or sell off the buying department to a bigger group. That could finish my job at 60 instead of 65. I can't control that, so I'd ask the union to get a clause on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger buyers, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn how the tool works, but also learn how a supplier thinks. Get on the phone and build relationships while you can. Take courses that employers pay for, and ask for them, because nobody offers.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long runway, and we should use it to fix pensions and retraining.
I'd tell younger buyers to **move early** into sturdier work.
think: I'd be fine: I retire at **65**, and the thinking work goes about when I'm gone.
My worry is for my **kids**, not me.
do: Carry on, use the tools when they help, and keep **clearing the mortgage**.
Talk with **Priya** about where she wants to go.
Join the **union committee** and push for training.
feel: **Calm**, with a slight guilt at being on the right side of the timeline.
S4.quote: Learn how the tool works, but also learn how a supplier thinks. Get on the phone and build relationships while you can.
fieldNote: Ten years reaches his **retirement**, so his job feels secure; only a sale of the firm could change that.
Wants to act as a **mentor** to the junior buyers.
He asks for a union clause on a sale, a precise worry from his private equity experience.

steps.text: Keep buying fittings and use the AI tools when they help
Join the union committee and push for training for younger buyers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to get the safety nets in place. What would help is a proper deal: retraining that employers or the state pay for, a pension that can't be raided, and a share of whatever the firm saves. I'd also like the owners to be honest with us about their plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not the kind of man who thinks technology is the enemy. I just think the people who get the savings should share them, and that's a fairness thing for me.

headlineQuote: I just think the people who get the savings should share them, and that's a fairness thing for me.
portrait: Hassan, 58, buys **pipe, valves and fittings** for a plumbing and heating wholesaler, and knows the plumbers by name.
He is progressive and **union-friendly**, and blames the private equity owners more than the technology.
Steady with new tools, he already uses the **forecast** now and then and would use it daily to stay useful.
He has about four months saved, six years of **mortgage** left, and a wife, Lena, whose wage steadies the household.
His moods follow the timeline: uneasy in the mild cases, **anxious** at two years, and calm when ten years reaches retirement.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because the safety nets would not exist in time and his job would go first.
whatWouldHelp: Employer-paid **retraining**, an untouchable **pension**, and a fair **share** of the savings.
